title: Eleven doors
hookLine: like a burning house with eleven doors, there are many ways out
carry: any door, opened with clear seeing

lines: IS THERE ONE THING THAT FREES THE MIND?
cards: Dasama, a householder from a town called Atthakanagara, comes to the city of Pataliputta on business. Business done, he travels on to Vesali, looking for the monk Ananda.
He has a single question, and he wants a single answer. Is there one thing, just one, which, if someone practices it diligently, frees the mind? He's hoping for the one key.

teach.h: ONE THING? YES, IN ELEVEN FORMS
teach.b: This is the fifty-second discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the man from Atthakanagara. Ananda answers: yes, there is one thing. Then he names it in eleven forms.

Someone enters the first meditative absorption and sees it clearly: this too is put together, made by intention, and whatever is made is impermanent and will end. Standing on that insight, the mind is freed.
The same with the second absorption, the third, the fourth.

The same with loving-kindness, compassion, gladness for others and equanimity, the four divine abodes. The same with three formless states: boundless space, boundless consciousness, and nothingness. Eleven in all.
The door isn't the state itself.

teach.h: SEE THAT EVEN THIS IS MADE
teach.b: It's seeing that even this lovely state is made, and so will pass. Dasama is overjoyed. It's as if, he says, a man looking for one entrance to a hidden treasure found eleven at once.

teach.h: A BURNING HOUSE WITH ELEVEN DOORS
teach.b: Or a man whose house has eleven doors: if it caught fire, he could escape through any one. Then he does something very practical.

He gathers the monks of Vesali and Pataliputta, feeds them with his own hands, gives each a pair of robes, gives Ananda a set of three robes, and has a dwelling built for him. There's a quiet comfort here.

Dasama wanted one way out, the right one, and found eleven. Some readers hear in it a path with doors for many kinds of minds: stillness, kindness, spaciousness. Any door, opened with clear seeing, leads out.

how: Buddhist meditation traditions offer many entry points, from breath-based concentration to loving-kindness and the other divine abodes, and some teachers match a practice to a student's temperament.

o: the gates of an old Indian city
ways out, each opened by seeing clearly
eleven rules every monk must keep

games.q: count the doors — tap the pairs.
p: seeing even this is made and will end

s: Ananda told Dasama there is only one way to free the mind
he said yes, there is one thing, and then named it in eleven forms.
the door is seeing that even a lovely state is made and will pass
the state itself isn't the exit; seeing it clearly is.
Dasama went home without giving anything
he fed the monks, gave them robes, and had a dwelling built for Ananda.

games.q: you're Dasama. you asked for one way to free the mind, and Ananda has shown you eleven. what do you say?
o: that's too many; I wanted one.
like a man looking for one entrance to a treasure who finds eleven at once.
games.why: Dasama is overjoyed: like one treasure entrance becoming eleven, or a burning house with eleven doors to escape by.

practice: Choose one of Ananda's doors for this sit, stillness with the breath, kindness toward someone, or the sense of open space around you, and settle into it until it's pleasant.
Then, gently, see what Dasama learned: this calm was made, by sitting, by breathing, by intention, and it will change. Rest in that seeing, without pushing the calm away.

wordCard.voice: Eleven doors. Four absorptions, four divine abodes, three formless states: each a way out of a burning house, when seen as made and passing.

orig.note: Pali dvara: door, gateway. Dasama's house has eleven dvara.

carryVoice: Your line: any door, opened with clear seeing. Nobody has to find the one right door. Day four hundred forty-four, done.
